content: The document outlines the guidelines for managing advanced HIV disease and the rapid initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART), as published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in July 2017. It provides detailed recommendations for addressing the challenges faced by patients presenting with advanced stages of HIV infection, defined as having a CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³ or being in WHO Clinical Stages 3 or 4. Despite global progress in scaling up ART access, a significant proportion of patients still present with advanced disease, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, where barriers to early diagnosis and care persist. The guidelines emphasize the high mortality rates among patients with advanced HIV disease, especially within the first three months of ART initiation. Common causes of death include co-infections such as tuberculosis (TB), cryptococcal meningitis, severe bacterial infections, and immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). Approximately 25% of patients globally begin ART with a CD4 count below 100 cells/mm³, with even higher rates in sub-Saharan Africa. WHO recommends several interventions to reduce mortality and morbidity in patients with advanced HIV disease. These include isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT) to prevent TB, co-trimoxazole prophylaxis, and screening for cryptococcal disease in patients with CD4 counts below 100 cells/mm³ in high-prevalence settings. Additionally, TB screening using urine LAM assays is advised. Recent studies have explored enhanced intervention packages, which combine infection prophylaxis, screening, and other care elements, to improve outcomes in this population. Two randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included in the systematic review to evaluate the effectiveness of these enhanced intervention packages. The first trial, REMSTART, conducted in Tanzania and Zambia, involved screening for cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) and TB using GeneXpert, followed by antifungal treatment and rapid ART initiation. Weekly adherence support visits were also provided. The second trial, REALITY, conducted in Malawi, Uganda, Zimbabwe, and Kenya, assessed an enhanced prophylaxis package that included co-trimoxazole, isoniazid, fluconazole, azithromycin, and albendazole, alongside ART. Both trials demonstrated significant reductions in all-cause mortality and hospitalizations among patients receiving the enhanced packages compared to standard care. The interventions were particularly effective in addressing co-infections and improving ART adherence. However, the REALITY trial found no additional benefit from supplementary food or raltegravir, which were excluded from further recommendations. The guidelines highlight the importance of implementing these enhanced care packages to address the unique needs of patients with advanced HIV disease. They also stress the need for continued efforts to overcome barriers to early diagnosis, linkage to care, and timely ART initiation to maximize the population-level benefits of ART.
